## Interpreting your results in a healthy way

- Results reflect your **recent** state (the past week for the DASS-21, the past
  month for the PSS-10), not who you are as a person; scores change with
  circumstances.

  balance between study and rest, not as a diagnostic label.

Academic stress in university students in Vietnam

## Common sources of stress for students in Vietnam

- **Exam and grade pressure**: packed exam schedules, fear of failing a course,
  outstanding credits, retaking subjects; GPA is tied to scholarships and job
  opportunities.
- **Assignment workload**: back-to-back deadlines, projects, essays and group
  assignments overlapping.
- **Family expectations**: the "other people's children" comparison, pressure to
  succeed so as not to let parents down, especially for students living away from
  home.
- **Financial pressure**: tuition, rent and living costs; many students work
  part-time on top of studying, cutting into their rest.
- **Peer pressure**: comparing yourself with friends on grades, internships,
  language certificates and extracurricular activities.
- **Transition to a new environment**: first-year students have to adapt to
  self-directed learning at university, living away from family, and building new
  relationships.
- **Career direction**: final-year students worry about internships, their thesis,
  job applications and life after graduation.

concentration, processing speed and emotional regulation — meaning you study less
effectively and get more stressed by the same amount of work.

## Pressure from family expectations

In Vietnamese culture, a child's academic achievement is often bound up with the
pride of the whole family. This can motivate, but it easily becomes a burden ("I'm
afraid of letting my parents down", "other people's children"). Some ways to cope:

- **Have a prepared, honest conversation**: pick a calm moment and explain
  specifically what your programme involves, how hard it is, and what your plans
  are; parents often base expectations on an outdated picture of university and
  will adjust once they understand the reality.
- **Set goals based on your own values**: separate "what I want" from "what others
  want for me"; set achievable academic goals matched to your abilities and a
  realistic career direction.
- **Share progress regularly**: update your family on both effort and difficulties
  rather than only reporting end-of-term results — this reduces the pressure of
  being judged purely on grades.

## DASS-21 (Depression Anxiety Stress Scales – 21 items)

The DASS-21 by Lovibond & Lovibond (1995) measures three negative emotional states
over the past week: **depression** (low mood, loss of interest, hopelessness),
**anxiety** (fear, physical reactions such as trembling and a racing heart) and
**stress** (difficulty relaxing, irritability, restlessness). Each subscale has 7
items answered 0–3; each subscale total is doubled and compared against
classification thresholds: Normal / Mild / Moderate / Severe / Extremely Severe.
A validated Vietnamese version of the scale also exists (Tran et al., 2013).

**Important note**: the DASS-21 is a *screening* instrument, not a diagnostic tool.
A high score suggests you should seek a specialist assessment; it does not mean you
have a mental disorder.

## Social comparison and social media

- Remember that social media is a highlight reel: people post successes and rarely
  post failures — comparing yourself with that image is an unfair comparison.
- Limit scrolling time (set app timers); unfollow accounts that make you feel bad
  about yourself.
- Practise "vertical comparison": compare yourself today with yourself last
  semester, rather than with other people.
- Write down 3 things you managed each week — the brain has a negativity bias, so
  progress needs to be recorded deliberately.

[04_sleep_and_study.md::2] Sleep hygiene tips for students

## Sleep hygiene tips for students

- Keep consistent bed and wake times, including at weekends (within about an hour).
- Bedroom or dorm room: dark, quiet, well ventilated; use an eye mask or earplugs
  if it is noisy.
- Avoid phone and laptop screens 30 minutes before bed; turn on a blue-light
  filter in the evening.
- No caffeine (coffee, milk tea, energy drinks) after 3pm.
- Do not study in bed — keep the bed for sleep so your brain builds the
  association.
- If you have been lying down for 20 minutes without sleeping: get up, do
  something gentle (read a paper book) until you feel sleepy, then go back to bed.
- A short 15–25 minute nap helps alertness; napping for more than an hour tends to
  cause restlessness at night.

## Why does sleep matter for students?

Sleep is when the brain consolidates memory: what you learn during the day is
written into long-term memory largely while you sleep. Sleep deprivation reduces
concentration, processing speed and emotional regulation — meaning you study less
effectively and get more stressed by the same amount of work.

## All-nighters: more harm than good

Many students stay up all night before an exam. Research shows that after one
sleepless night, memory and reasoning decline by an amount comparable to the
impairment caused by a blood alcohol level above the drink-driving limit. Revising
for 4 hours and then sleeping properly is usually more effective than revising for
8 hours through the night.

## Group 2: Looking after your body

- **Sleep**: keep consistent bed and wake times, aiming for 7–8 hours a night;
  avoid screens 30 minutes before bed; no caffeine after 3pm. Sleep deprivation
  markedly reduces memory and increases the stress response.
- **Exercise**: 20–30 minutes a day (brisk walking, running, cycling, badminton,
  the gym); exercise releases endorphins and lowers the stress hormone cortisol.
- **Eat regularly**: do not skip meals during exam periods; limit energy drinks;
  drink enough water.

## Group 3: Regulating emotions

  repeat 4 times — useful right before an exam or when you feel keyed up.

  get the thoughts out of your head and see the problem more objectively.
- **Mindfulness**: spend 5–10 minutes observing your breath; a meditation app can
  help.
- **Limit social media**: set specific time windows; constantly comparing yourself
  with other people's images of success increases anxiety.

## PSS-10 (Perceived Stress Scale – 10 items)

Cohen's PSS-10 measures how far a person *perceives* their life over the past month
as unpredictable, uncontrollable and overloaded. The 10 items are answered on a 0–4
scale (Never → Very often); the positively worded items (4, 5, 7, 8) are reverse
scored. The total runs 0–40: 0–13 low, 14–26 moderate, 27–40 high.

Unlike the DASS-21 (which measures *symptoms*), the PSS-10 measures *subjective
perception* of stress — two complementary perspectives, so it is worth combining
both in a self-assessment.

## DASS-21 (Depression Anxiety Stress Scales – 21 items)

The DASS-21 by Lovibond & Lovibond (1995) measures three negative emotional states
over the past week: **depression** (low mood, loss of interest, hopelessness),
**anxiety** (fear, physical reactions such as trembling and a racing heart) and
**stress** (difficulty relaxing, irritability, restlessness). Each subscale has 7
items answered 0–3; each subscale total is doubled and compared against
classification thresholds: Normal / Mild / Moderate / Severe / Extremely Severe.
A validated Vietnamese version of the scale also exists (Tran et al., 2013).

**Important note**: the DASS-21 is a *screening* instrument, not a diagnostic tool.
A high score suggests you should seek a specialist assessment; it does not mean you
have a mental disorder.

## Financial pressure and part-time work

- Build a simple monthly budget (rent, food, study costs, a buffer) and track
  spending with an app or a notebook.
- Look into **scholarships, tuition waivers and student loans** through the Student
  Affairs Office — many support schemes are little known.
- If you work part-time: prioritise flexible hours close to your campus or home;
  cap your total hours (roughly under 20 a week) so work does not eat into study
  and sleep.
- Work related to your field (teaching assistance, paid internships, freelance work
  in your discipline) provides income and experience at the same time.
